description: Team LunaSight is six students building a web tool that helps compare lunar south-pole landing sites and dates using NASA data. I'm Rohit Bansal, the team's Leader. We're looking for people skilled in Plotly, Leaflet, PyProj, or Git. Beginners are welcome. Message us if you're interested!
summary: LunaSight is a decision-support tool for choosing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates. It uses JPL Horizons ephemeris for the Sun and Earth, and NASA's LOLA elevation data to compute terrain horizons, so a ridge that blocks the Sun or Earth is reflected in the results. Users can compare site and date options, run launch-delay scenarios, and see sunlit hours, darkness periods, Earth visibility and communication blackouts, with each output labelled as an estimate and linked to its source. An AI assistant explains the results for learners and educators, and answers "what if" questions by running new calculations rather than guessing. This matters because south-pole missions face low sunlight and intermittent Earth contact, and planners need to re-evaluate options quickly when schedules slip. LunaSight makes those trade-offs clear and traceable, while stating what it does not measure, such as boulder hazards and radio link budgets.
details:
What it does and how it works

LunaSight helps mission planners, educators and learners compare lunar south-pole landing sites and dates. A user picks a preset site or enters coordinates, sets a start time and duration, and the tool computes where the Sun and Earth are in the sky at each 10-minute step. It then checks those positions against the local terrain horizon, built from NASA’s LOLA elevation data, to decide whether the Sun or Earth is visible or blocked. From this it reports sunlit hours, longest darkness, Earth-visible hours and the longest communication blackout. A launch-delay simulator reruns the calculation for +1 day, +7 days or one lunar cycle, and a comparison view shows the results side by side. An AI assistant answers questions from the project documents and explains the computed results.

Benefits

Planners can see how a small change in date or site affects power and communication without working through several complex NASA tools. Educators get a clear way to explain why the south pole is hard to reach and power, using real geometry. Every output is labelled as an estimate and linked to its data source, so users can see what the numbers are based on and what they do not cover.

Intended impact

The aim is faster, clearer decisions during mission planning, especially when schedules or hardware change, and better public understanding of lunar engineering challenges. The tool is designed to support planners, not replace mission-safety analysis.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Plotly.js for charts, Leaflet for the 2D map, and Three.js as an optional 3D view
  • Science engine: Python with FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio for DEM processing, and PyProj for coordinate transforms
  • Data: JPL Horizons API for ephemeris, LOLA south-pole DEM (LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ) for terrain, and JSON files for results
  • AI assistant: an LLM API with function calling, connected to three tools: get_site_analysis, run_delay_scenario and search_docs
  • Tools and hosting: Git and GitHub for version control, and a local or single cloud host for the demo
  • Hardware: standard laptops; no specialised hardware was required

Creativity

The main creative choice is terrain-adjusted visibility. Many lunar tools treat the horizon as flat, which misses the ridges and crater rims that block sunlight at the pole. The tool also separates geometric Earth visibility from a working radio link, so results are not overstated. The delay simulator turns “what if” questions into real recalculations, and the Planner and Educator views present the same results at different levels of detail.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific honesty: outputs are labelled as estimates, and limits such as the 20 m terrain resolution and the lack of link-budget analysis are stated.
  • Scope and time: the team limited the first version to one site and one 24-hour window, then planned expansion once results were validated, given the three-day deadline.
  • Accessibility: two audiences, planners and learners, were considered in the interface and the AI explanations.
  • Team skills and roles: work was split into science engine, frontend, and API and AI, with shared agreements on coordinate conventions, units and data format from the start.
  • Reliability: the team identified the main integration risks early, including coordinate and timestamp conventions, and planned validation before expanding the work.
